newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bombing trial juror is anti-death penalty.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bombing trial juror is anti-death penalty.

text.p: A potential juror in the Oklahoma City bombing trial who has withheld taxes because she is a pacifist told the court Monday she was unalterably opposed to the death penalty.
"I could not consider the death penalty," the substitute school teacher and mother of two said as the third week of jury selection got under way.
Another woman who gave long and deliberate answers said seeing the movie "I Want to Live!" left her "traumatized" and totally opposed to the death penalty.

However, as she grew older the mother of four became more accepting of the death penalty. The 1958 movie for which Susan Hayward won an Academy Award was about a woman wrongly accused of committing murder.
The woman, who works with patients with respiratory problems, also had at her fingertips a number of details about the bombing that have escaped other jury candidates.
A third potential juror said it was doubtful he could think of any reasons for not voting for the death penalty if a murder were premeditated.

The judge, prosecutors and defence attorneys have been questioning potential jurors on a wide range of topics including opposition to the death penalty and attitudes toward the federal government as they select a jury of 12 plus six alternates to decide the fate of Timothy McVeigh.
Six potential jurors were interviewed on Monday, bringing the total to 67.
The 28-year-old Gulf War veteran was charged with bombing the Alfred P. Murrah federal building April 19, 1995, killing 168 people. He has pleaded not guilty and faces the death penalty if convicted.
McVeigh paid close attention to the proceedings as he has throughout, looking at file folders and passing notes to his attorneys.

The tax protester said she and her husband have in the past withheld taxes because of their opposition to military spending. Her husband's wages were currently being garnished, the 63rd prospective juror said.
As has been customary, Federal Judge Richard Matsch did not tell her if she would be excused from serving on the trial, which is expected to last about four months.
Potential jurors were also being asked about their exposure to pre-trial publicity about the high-profile case.

An outdoorsman who works on a production line at a factory told the court he reads only the Sunday newspaper and plays with his dogs when he comes home from work rather than watch television news. He said he could vote for the death penalty if McVeigh were convicted.
Only four potential jurors have been dismissed publicly, including a woman with stress problems and a man who did not meet the one-year residency requirement.
Each day the judge and lawyers for both sides meet in a closed-door conference to review the jurors. Some are being excused for particular reasons but the decisions are not being made public.
